Luminous, rich colours; crisp focal details on the face and costume, softer painted edges toward the distance. No flat single-tone cel shading, photographic appearance, semi-realistic face or plastic 3D-render finish. Keep this rendering exactly as in the attached image — the same finish, line, shading, skin and colour treatment.

Time of day: warm lamplight or candlelight indoors, the rest in shadow.

Outfit: a piercer look fitted to her body — a cropped black tank top, low-rise cargo trousers, a studded belt and small rings along her ears, showing her shoulders, collarbones and legs as far as the outfit allows, following her curvy figure — a slim waist and rounded hips; intimate areas covered.
POSTURE: standing at a waist-high railing or sill.
COMPOSITION: a waist-up shot of her head, torso and hands; body in side profile, her face in profile too, not turned toward the camera, facing the right of the frame, so her own right side is toward the camera; camera at her eye level; she is placed in the left third of the frame, open space of the place to her right.

RIGHT HAND: her own right hand is in PROP — her near arm, on the camera side.

PROP: with her own right hand she holds a tray of rainbow-anodized studs at chest height; it is all she holds.
GAZE: her eyes rest on what she holds.
EXPRESSION: level brow, calm unhurried eyes, mouth closed and composed.
Scene note: she is the piercer choosing a rainbow-anodized ring for a client

Framing: a waist-up shot — the bottom edge crosses her waist; hips, legs and feet are out of frame.

Leave behind everything she wears in the attached image — no crown, tiara, helmet, feathers, headpiece, hairpins from it, armour or regalia; her hair is styled for the everyday outfit, with at most one small accessory.

Her element — niobium: a soft, grey, ductile metal first found in 1801 in a heavy black stone from New England kept in a London museum and called columbium; long thought the same as tantalum, it was split from it in 1844 and named for Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, who wept for her fourteen lost children until she turned to a stone that still weeps on a mountainside; an electric current grows a thin oxide on it that shines blue, violet, gold or green by its thickness, used for body jewellery; cooled near absolute zero it carries current without resistance in the great superconducting magnets of scanners and particle accelerators — may show in the outfit's details, motifs or small accessories.
